title: Nirvana Day
hookLine: February 15 in East Asia: the Buddha's passing remembered

cards: In a temple in Japan in mid-February, a huge painted scroll is unrolled and hung. In the middle, a man lies on his right side between trees, head resting on his hand. Around him, crowds are weeping: monks, kings, gods.
And animals. An elephant on its back. A tiger.
Birds, a snake, a crowd of creatures. It's called a nehan-zu, a picture of nirvana. And it isn't a picture of awakening.
It's a picture of a death.

teach.b: Buddhists use the word nirvana for two things. One is the awakening itself, the fire of craving going out, which yesterday remembered.
The other is what happens when an awakened one dies: the final nirvana, parinirvana in Sanskrit, parinibbana in Pali. Nothing is left to be reborn. Nirvana Day remembers that second one.
In Japan it's usually kept on February 15; other Mahayana communities keep it then too, or on February 8, or by the lunar calendar.
In Theravada lands, the passing is kept on Vesak, with the birth and the awakening. Same event, different calendars. Now the story, from the Book of the Great Decease.
The Buddha is eighty, and ill.

He walks to Kusinara, a small town, and lies down between two sal trees. The text says the trees burst into flower out of season and dropped blossoms on him. His cousin Ananda goes off and weeps against a doorpost.
The Buddha calls him back: hadn't he always taught that everything dear must change and part? Then he asks the monks three times if anyone has a last doubt. Nobody speaks.

teach.h: THE LAST WORDS AS A LESSON.
teach.b: And then his last words, in Rhys Davids's translation: "Decay is inherent in all component things! Work out your salvation with diligence!" He doesn't hide his death.
He uses it as the final lesson. On Nirvana Day, temples chant, read the story and sit; some make little dumplings or rice cakes. The point isn't grief.
It's looking straight at an ending, with company.

how: In Japan and many Mahayana communities, temples mark Nirvana Day (Nehan-e) around February 15 by hanging a painting of the Buddha's passing, chanting, and reading from the account of his last days; Theravada Buddhists remember the passing on Vesak.

it remembers his passing, the final nirvana; the awakening was yesterday's Rohatsu.

games.q: you are the Buddha, dying. your closest friend is sobbing outside. what do you do?
o: call him back and remind him all dear things change.
games.why: he calls Ananda back, comforts him, praises his years of care, and reminds him that whatever is dear must change and part.

practice: Let one ending come to mind, not the hardest one you know: a school, a house, a friendship that drifted, a pet, a season of life.
Look at it the way the scroll looks at the Buddha, plainly, with company around, and if grief comes, let it sit with you too; Ananda wept.
At the end, come back to this breath, which is also ending, and the next one, which is beginning.

wordCard.voice: Nirvana Day. February 15 in East Asian Buddhism, remembering the Buddha's final passing, his parinirvana between the sal trees. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit parinirvana: complete going-out, the final nirvana at an awakened one's death; Pali parinibbana.

carryVoice: Your line: all things end. Even a Buddha's life came to a close. See you tomorrow.
